2 Simulation and Fitting Settings

This demo uses the fixed representative dataset and fitted Bayesian models distributed with the vignette. These files are stored under vignettes/articles/resources/demo_brms_HNB_nl so that the rendered example uses the same data as the manuscript rather than a user-specific local directory.

The goal is not to reproduce a full simulation study. Instead, the file shows a compact workflow: load the paper dataset, load the saved Bayesian model fits, compute posterior and ISCV Z-residuals, compare them with PPC and HPC diagnostics, and summarize the resulting diagnostic p-values.

Code
# Fixed sample size used by the paper dataset distributed with this vignette.
n_sample <- 50

sample_tag <- paste0("N", n_sample)
file_tag <- paste0("_n", n_sample)

# One representative dataset only. This is not a 500-replication run.
representative_id <- 1L
force_recalc <- FALSE
force_refit <- force_recalc
force_rerun <- force_recalc
force_recompute_zres <- force_recalc
force_recompute_ppc_hpc <- force_recalc

# Holdout proportion for the single-dataset HPC calculation.
test_prop <- 0.20

# Data-generating parameters from the simulation code.
beta0 <- -5
beta1 <- c(0.6, -5)

alpha0 <- -1
alpha1 <- c(6, 1)

true_size <- 4

x1_min <- 0.5
x1_max <- 15


brms_backend <- "rstan"
brms_cores <- 1
brms_chains <- 4
brms_iter <- 2000
brms_warmup <- 1000

ndraws_use <- 2000
seed_use <- 20260511
x_check <- c("lp", "x1")

# Number of auxiliary randomizations for a single discrete-response dataset.
# This is not the number of simulated datasets.
nrep_z <- 500

options(mc.cores = brms_cores)

if (requireNamespace("rstan", quietly = TRUE)) {
  rstan::rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
}

make_k_anova <- function(n_test) {
  as.integer(max(3L, min(10L, floor(n_test / 5))))
}

hnb_family <- brms::hurdle_negbinomial(
  link = "log",
  link_shape = "identity",
  link_hu = "logit"
)

nb_family <- brms::negbinomial(
  link = "log",
  link_shape = "identity"
)

required_cols <- c(
  "y", "x1", "x2",
  "z1", "z2", "z3", "z4", "z5",
  "zeros"
)

3 Diagnostic Goal and Candidate Models

This example uses data generated from a logarithmic hurdle negative binomial (HNB) model and then fits four candidate Bayesian models to the same dataset. The first model is the data-generating model, while the other three deliberately introduce different types of misspecification:

  1. HNB-log: true response family and true logarithmic functional form.
  2. HNB-linear: true response family but wrong linear functional form for x1.
  3. NB-log: wrong response family. Although the count mean uses a logarithmic term, the omitted hurdle zero/count mechanism can be projected into the NB mean structure, so the effective functional form can also be misspecified.
  4. NB-linear: wrong response family and wrong linear functional form for x1.

The purpose is to show how different diagnostics respond to different types of model deficiency. Overall checks such as Z-SW assess whether the residual distribution is close to standard normal, while the targeted Z-AOV test against x1 checks whether the residual mean varies systematically across the covariate. PPC and HPC are included as predictive-check comparisons based on analogous residual summaries.

Because the response is discrete, RSP Z-residuals use auxiliary randomization. In this demo, each fitted model is evaluated using nrep_z = 500 repeated auxiliary randomizations. The replicated Z-residual p-values are shown as histograms and summarized by the distribution-free upper-bound p-value.

4 Data-Generating Model

For each observation, generate

X_{i,1}\sim \mathrm{Unif}(0.5,15),\qquad X_{i,2}\sim \mathrm{Binom}(1,0.5),

and five independent nuisance covariates

Z_{i,j}\sim N(0,1),\qquad j=1,\ldots,5.

The data are generated from a hurdle negative binomial model. The positive-count component has mean

\log(\mu_i)=\alpha_0+\alpha_1\log(X_{i,1})+\alpha_2X_{i,2},

and the hurdle, or zero-probability, component is

\mathrm{logit}(\pi_i^0)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i,1}+\beta_2X_{i,2}.

The executable settings used in this demo are

\alpha_0=-1,\qquad \alpha_1=6,\qquad \alpha_2=1,

\beta_0=-5,\qquad \beta_1=0.6,\qquad \beta_2=-5,

with negative-binomial size parameter

\mathrm{size}=4.

The nuisance Z variables are generated with true coefficient zero and are included in fitted models to match the simulation-code structure.

5 Resource and Fitting Utilities

The code below defines helper functions for reading the fixed dataset and saved brms fits from resources. It also keeps a small refitting helper for holdout fits if those fits are not included in the resource file. The Z-residual, plotting, PPC, and HPC diagnostics later in the demo are called directly from Zresidual.

Code
fit_or_read_brms <- function(
  file,
  formula,
  data,
  seed,
  family,
  prior,
  chains = brms_chains,
  iter = brms_iter,
  warmup = brms_warmup
) {
  if (!force_refit && file.exists(file)) {
    return(readRDS(file))
  }

  fit <- brms::brm(
    formula = formula,
    family = family,
    prior = prior,
    data = data,
    backend = brms_backend,
    refresh = 0,
    cores = brms_cores,
    chains = chains,
    iter = iter,
    warmup = warmup,
    seed = seed,
    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12),
    save_pars = brms::save_pars(all = TRUE)
  )

  saveRDS(fit, file = file)
  fit
}

read_resource_rds <- function(file, label = "resource") {
  if (!file.exists(file)) {
    stop("Cannot find ", label, ": ", file, call. = FALSE)
  }
  readRDS(file)
}

normalize_resource_name <- function(x) {
  gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "", tolower(x))
}

list_resource_names <- function(x, prefix = character()) {
  if (!is.list(x) || inherits(x, "brmsfit")) return(character())

  nms <- names(x)
  if (is.null(nms)) nms <- rep("", length(x))

  out <- character()
  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    this_name <- if (nzchar(nms[i])) nms[i] else paste0("[[", i, "]]")
    this_path <- paste(c(prefix, this_name), collapse = "$")
    out <- c(out, this_path)

    if (is.list(x[[i]]) && !inherits(x[[i]], "brmsfit")) {
      out <- c(out, list_resource_names(x[[i]], c(prefix, this_name)))
    }
  }

  out
}

get_resource_object <- function(x, candidates, label, required = TRUE) {
  candidates_norm <- normalize_resource_name(candidates)

  search_one <- function(obj) {
    if (!is.list(obj) || inherits(obj, "brmsfit")) return(NULL)

    nms <- names(obj)
    if (!is.null(nms)) {
      nms_norm <- normalize_resource_name(nms)
      idx <- match(candidates_norm, nms_norm, nomatch = 0L)
      idx <- idx[idx > 0L]
      if (length(idx)) return(obj[[idx[1L]]])
    }

    for (ii in seq_along(obj)) {
      if (is.list(obj[[ii]]) && !inherits(obj[[ii]], "brmsfit")) {
        ans <- search_one(obj[[ii]])
        if (!is.null(ans)) return(ans)
      }
    }

    NULL
  }

  ans <- search_one(x)

  if (is.null(ans) && isTRUE(required)) {
    available <- list_resource_names(x)
    stop(
      "Could not find ", label, " in the saved resource object.
",
      "Tried names: ", paste(candidates, collapse = ", "), "
",
      "Available names include: ", paste(utils::head(available, 40), collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  ans
}

get_resource_fit <- function(x, candidates, label, required = TRUE) {
  ans <- get_resource_object(x, candidates = candidates, label = label, required = required)

  if (!is.null(ans) && !inherits(ans, "brmsfit")) {
    stop(
      label, " was found, but it is not a `brmsfit` object. ",
      "Please check the saved fits file.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  ans
}
Code
zresid_chisq_pvalue <- function(zres, df) {
  if (is.list(zres) && !is.null(zres$zresidual)) {
    zres <- zres$zresidual
  }

  zmat <- as.matrix(zres)
  storage.mode(zmat) <- "numeric"

  pvals <- apply(
    zmat,
    2,
    function(z) stats::pchisq(sum(z^2, na.rm = TRUE), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)
  )

  Zresidual::upper_bound_pvalue(pvals)
}

sim_id <- representative_id

dat_hnb <- read_resource_rds(data_file, label = "fixed paper dataset")

# Keep these derived columns available even if the saved dataset only stores the minimal variables.
if (!"log_x1" %in% names(dat_hnb)) {

7 Fit HNB-log and HNB-linear Models

Both HNB models have the same hurdle component. They differ only in the count-component functional form of x1.

Code
hnb_prior <- c(
  brms::prior(normal(0, 10), class = "Intercept"),
  brms::prior(normal(0, 10), class = "b"),
  brms::prior(normal(0, 10), class = "Intercept", dpar = "hu"),
  brms::prior(normal(0, 10), class = "b", dpar = "hu"),
  brms::prior(exponential(1), class = "shape")
)

formula_log_hnb <- brms::bf(
  y ~ log_x1 + x2 + z1 + z2 + z3 + z4 + z5,
  hu ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2 + z3 + z4 + z5
)

formula_linear_hnb <- brms::bf(
  y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2 + z3 + z4 + z5,
  hu ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2 + z3 + z4 + z5
)

fits_full_resource <- read_resource_rds(
  fits_full_file,
  label = "saved full-data model fits"
)

fit_log_hnb <- get_resource_fit(
  fits_full_resource,
  candidates = c("fit_log_hnb", "log_hnb", "hnb_log", "HNB_log", "HNB-log", "fit_hnb_log"),
  label = "HNB-log full-data fit"
)

fit_linear_hnb <- get_resource_fit(
  fits_full_resource,
  candidates = c("fit_linear_hnb", "linear_hnb", "hnb_linear", "HNB_linear", "HNB-linear", "fit_hnb_linear"),
  label = "HNB-linear full-data fit"
)

8 Fit NB-log and NB-linear Comparison Models

These two comparison models are fitted to the same HNB-generated dataset. The NB-log model keeps the logarithmic functional form for x1 but uses the wrong response family. The NB-linear model uses the wrong response family and the wrong functional form.

Code
nb_prior <- c(
  brms::prior(normal(0, 10), class = "Intercept"),
  brms::prior(normal(0, 10), class = "b"),
  brms::prior(exponential(1), class = "shape")
)

formula_log_nb <- brms::bf(
  y ~ log_x1 + x2 + z1 + z2 + z3 + z4 + z5
)

formula_linear_nb <- brms::bf(
  y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2 + z3 + z4 + z5
)

fit_log_nb <- get_resource_fit(
  fits_full_resource,
  candidates = c("fit_log_nb", "log_nb", "nb_log", "NB_log", "NB-log", "fit_nb_log"),

)

fit_linear_nb <- get_resource_fit(
  fits_full_resource,
  candidates = c("fit_linear_nb", "linear_nb", "nb_linear", "NB_linear", "NB-linear", "fit_nb_linear"),
  label = "NB-linear full-data fit"
)

9 Holdout Fits for PPC/HPC Comparisons

The PPC checks use the full-data fits. The HPC checks use a deterministic 20% holdout split and refit each candidate model on the training subset. This gives a compact comparison between residual-based diagnostics and predictive-check diagnostics for the same four candidate models.

Code
fits_hpc_resource <- if (file.exists(fits_hpc_file)) {
  read_resource_rds(fits_hpc_file, label = "saved holdout model fits")
} else {
  fits_full_resource
}

hpc_split <- get_resource_object(
  fits_hpc_resource,
  candidates = c("hpc_split", "holdout_split", "split_hpc", "data_split"),
  label = "HPC holdout split",
  required = FALSE
)

if (!is.null(hpc_split)) {
  dat_hnb_train <- hpc_split$train
  dat_hnb_test  <- hpc_split$test
} else {
  set.seed(seed_use + 50000 + sim_id)
  n_test <- max(1L, floor(test_prop * nrow(dat_hnb)))
  test_id <- sort(sample(seq_len(nrow(dat_hnb)), size = n_test))
  dat_hnb_train <- dat_hnb[-test_id, , drop = FALSE]
  dat_hnb_test  <- dat_hnb[ test_id, , drop = FALSE]
}

fit_log_hnb_hpc <- get_resource_fit(
  fits_hpc_resource,
  candidates = c("fit_log_hnb_hpc", "log_hnb_hpc", "hnb_log_hpc", "HNB_log_hpc", "HNB-log-hpc"),
  label = "HNB-log holdout fit",
  required = FALSE
)

if (is.null(fit_log_hnb_hpc)) {
  fit_log_hnb_hpc <- fit_or_read_brms(
    file = file.path(resources_path, paste0("fit_log_hnb_hpc", file_tag, "_sim", sim_id, ".rds")),
    formula = formula_log_hnb,
    data = dat_hnb_train,
    seed = seed_use + 60000 + sim_id,
    family = hnb_family,
    prior = hnb_prior
  )
}

fit_linear_hnb_hpc <- get_resource_fit(
  fits_hpc_resource,
  candidates = c("fit_linear_hnb_hpc", "linear_hnb_hpc", "hnb_linear_hpc", "HNB_linear_hpc", "HNB-linear-hpc"),
  label = "HNB-linear holdout fit",

)

if (is.null(fit_linear_hnb_hpc)) {

10 Compute Posterior and ISCV RSP Z-residuals

The response is discrete, so RSP Z-residuals depend on auxiliary randomization. Here nrep_z = 500 means 500 auxiliary randomizations for this one fixed dataset, not 500 simulated datasets.

Code
zres_post_file <- file.path(
  resources_path,
  paste0("zres_post_list_all_", sample_tag, ".rds")
)

zres_iscv_file <- file.path(
  resources_path,
  paste0("zres_iscv_list_all_", sample_tag, ".rds")
)

if (
  !force_recompute_zres &&
    file.exists(zres_post_file) &&
    file.exists(zres_iscv_file)
) {
  zres_post_list <- readRDS(zres_post_file)
  zres_iscv_list <- readRDS(zres_iscv_file)

} else {
  z_hnb_log_post <- Zresidual::Zresidual(
    fit_log_hnb,
    data = dat_hnb,
    mcmc_summarize = "post",
    nrep = nrep_z
  )

  z_hnb_linear_post <- Zresidual::Zresidual(
    fit_linear_hnb,
    data = dat_hnb,
    mcmc_summarize = "post",
    nrep = nrep_z
  )

  z_nb_log_post <- Zresidual::Zresidual(
    fit_log_nb,
    data = dat_hnb,
    mcmc_summarize = "post",
    nrep = nrep_z
  )

  z_nb_linear_post <- Zresidual::Zresidual(
    fit_linear_nb,
    data = dat_hnb,
    mcmc_summarize = "post",
    nrep = nrep_z
  )

  z_hnb_log_iscv <- Zresidual::Zresidual(
    fit_log_hnb,
    data = dat_hnb,
    mcmc_summarize = "iscv",
    nrep = nrep_z
  )

  z_hnb_linear_iscv <- Zresidual::Zresidual(
    fit_linear_hnb,
    data = dat_hnb,
    mcmc_summarize = "iscv",
    nrep = nrep_z
  )

  z_nb_log_iscv <- Zresidual::Zresidual(
    fit_log_nb,
    data = dat_hnb,
    mcmc_summarize = "iscv",
    nrep = nrep_z
  )

  z_nb_linear_iscv <- Zresidual::Zresidual(
    fit_linear_nb,
    data = dat_hnb,
    mcmc_summarize = "iscv",
    nrep = nrep_z
  )

  zres_post_list <- list(
    HNB_log = z_hnb_log_post,
    HNB_linear = z_hnb_linear_post,
    NB_log = z_nb_log_post,
    NB_linear = z_nb_linear_post
  )

  zres_iscv_list <- list(
    HNB_log = z_hnb_log_iscv,
    HNB_linear = z_hnb_linear_iscv,
    NB_log = z_nb_log_iscv,
    NB_linear = z_nb_linear_iscv
  )

  saveRDS(zres_post_list, zres_post_file)
  saveRDS(zres_iscv_list, zres_iscv_file)
}

# Unpack named lists back to the object names used later in the vignette
z_hnb_log_post    <- zres_post_list$HNB_log
z_hnb_linear_post <- zres_post_list$HNB_linear
z_nb_log_post     <- zres_post_list$NB_log
z_nb_linear_post  <- zres_post_list$NB_linear

z_hnb_log_iscv    <- zres_iscv_list$HNB_log
z_hnb_linear_iscv <- zres_iscv_list$HNB_linear
z_nb_log_iscv     <- zres_iscv_list$NB_log
z_nb_linear_iscv  <- zres_iscv_list$NB_linear

zcov_hnb_log    <- Zresidual::Zcov(fit_log_hnb,    data = dat_hnb)
zcov_hnb_linear <- Zresidual::Zcov(fit_linear_hnb, data = dat_hnb)
zcov_nb_log     <- Zresidual::Zcov(fit_log_nb,     data = dat_hnb)
zcov_nb_linear  <- Zresidual::Zcov(fit_linear_nb,  data = dat_hnb)

fits_full <- list(
  HNB_log = fit_log_hnb,
  HNB_linear = fit_linear_hnb,
  NB_log = fit_log_nb,
  NB_linear = fit_linear_nb
)

p_eff <- vapply(
  fits_full,
  function(fit) loo::loo(fit)$estimates["p_loo", "Estimate"],
  numeric(1L)
)

df_post <- vapply(
  names(zres_post_list),
  function(mm) max(1, nrow(as.matrix(zres_post_list[[mm]])) - p_eff[[mm]]),
  numeric(1L)
)

df_iscv <- vapply(
  zres_iscv_list,
  function(zres) nrow(as.matrix(zres)),
  numeric(1L)
)

# Plot-only helper: force zero/count display without changing package functions
add_zero_indicator_for_plot <- function(zres, y) {
  z_plot <- zres
  attr(z_plot, "type") <- "hurdle"
  attr(z_plot, "zero_id") <- which(y == 0L)
  z_plot
}

z_hnb_log_post_plot    <- add_zero_indicator_for_plot(z_hnb_log_post, dat_hnb$y)

11 Visual Z-residual Diagnostics for the HNB Models

The first diagnostic view compares posterior RSP Z-residuals against x1 for the HNB-log and HNB-linear models. The HNB-log model is the data-generating model and should not show a systematic residual mean pattern. The HNB-linear model keeps the correct response family but uses a wrong linear functional form, so a residual pattern against x1 is expected. LOWESS curves are omitted because the visual and numerical conclusions rely on the residual points, binned boxplots, and diagnostic p-values rather than on a smoothing algorithm.

Code
irep_plot <- 1

op <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 1, 0), cex = 1.02)

plot(

  zcov = zcov_hnb_log,
  x_axis_var = "x1",
  irep = irep_plot,
  add_lowess = TRUE,

)

  z_hnb_log_post,

  x_axis_var = "x1",
  irep = irep_plot,
  num.bin = k_anova_full,
  k.test = k_anova_full,
  main.title = expression("(b) HNB Log, " * Z^"Post-RSP" * " Boxplot")
)

  x_axis_var = "x1",
  irep = irep_plot,

12 Visual Z-residual Diagnostics for the NB Comparison Models

The second diagnostic view shows the NB-log and NB-linear comparison models. For the NB-log model, the response family is misspecified because the data were generated from a hurdle negative binomial process. In the HNB data-generating process, the probability of entering the count component changes with the covariate. When a standard NB model is fitted without an explicit hurdle component, this zero/count mechanism can be projected into the NB mean structure. Therefore, an AOV rejection against x1 for the NB-log model is informative and should not be interpreted as a contradiction. Points in the scatterplots are grouped by the observed zero-count indicator for both NB models, because separation or over-abundance of small residuals among zero observations is informative about errors in the zero-count mechanism.

Code

)

)

14 Replicated Z-residual p-value Histograms

For discrete responses, RSP Z-residuals depend on the auxiliary randomization used to smooth the probability mass at each observed count. Therefore, the same fitted model can produce a distribution of diagnostic p-values across repeated auxiliary randomizations. Here we use nrep_z = 500 replicated Z-residual p-values for each model and show two diagnostics: the overall Z-SW test and the targeted Z-AOV test against x1.

The vertical line in each histogram marks the distribution-free upper-bound p-value used as the single-number summary in the table below. The HNB-log model is the true model. The HNB-linear model represents a wrong functional form under the correct HNB response family. The NB-log and NB-linear models illustrate how response-family misspecification can also induce apparent covariate-specific residual structure when the omitted hurdle zero/count mechanism is projected into the NB mean structure.

Code
post_sw_pvals <- list(
  `HNB-log` = sw.test.zresid(z_hnb_log_post),
  `HNB-linear` = sw.test.zresid(z_hnb_linear_post),
  `NB-log` = sw.test.zresid(z_nb_log_post),
  `NB-linear` = sw.test.zresid(z_nb_linear_post)
)

post_aov_x1_pvals <- list(
  `HNB-log` = aov.test.zresid(z_hnb_log_post, X = "x1", zcov = zcov_hnb_log, k_anova = k_anova_full),
  `HNB-linear` = aov.test.zresid(z_hnb_linear_post, X = "x1", zcov = zcov_hnb_linear, k_anova = k_anova_full),
  `NB-log` = aov.test.zresid(z_nb_log_post, X = "x1", zcov = zcov_nb_log, k_anova = k_anova_full),
  `NB-linear` = aov.test.zresid(z_nb_linear_post, X = "x1", zcov = zcov_nb_linear, k_anova = k_anova_full)
)

post_sw_ub <- vapply(post_sw_pvals, Zresidual::upper_bound_pvalue, numeric(1L))
post_aov_x1_ub <- vapply(post_aov_x1_pvals, Zresidual::upper_bound_pvalue, numeric(1L))

plot_hist_pvalues <- function(pvals, ub, main) {
  pvals <- pvals[is.finite(pvals)]
  hist(
    pvals,
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.05),
    xlim = c(0, 1),
    main = main,
    xlab = "Replicated p-values",
    ylab = "Frequency",
    col = "grey85",
    border = "white"
  )
  abline(v = ub, col = "red", lwd = 2)
  abline(v = 0.05, lty = 2, lwd = 1)
  legend(
    "topright",
    legend = paste0("UB = ", sprintf("%.3f", ub)),
    bty = "n",
    cex = 0.85
  )
}

op <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 1, 0), cex = 1.0)

plot_hist_pvalues(post_sw_pvals[["HNB-log"]], post_sw_ub[["HNB-log"]], "(a) HNB-log: Z-SW")
plot_hist_pvalues(post_sw_pvals[["HNB-linear"]], post_sw_ub[["HNB-linear"]], "(b) HNB-linear: Z-SW")
plot_hist_pvalues(post_sw_pvals[["NB-log"]], post_sw_ub[["NB-log"]], "(c) NB-log: Z-SW")
plot_hist_pvalues(post_sw_pvals[["NB-linear"]], post_sw_ub[["NB-linear"]], "(d) NB-linear: Z-SW")

plot_hist_pvalues(post_aov_x1_pvals[["HNB-log"]], post_aov_x1_ub[["HNB-log"]], "(e) HNB-log: Z-AOV-X1")
plot_hist_pvalues(post_aov_x1_pvals[["HNB-linear"]], post_aov_x1_ub[["HNB-linear"]], "(f) HNB-linear: Z-AOV-X1")
plot_hist_pvalues(post_aov_x1_pvals[["NB-log"]], post_aov_x1_ub[["NB-log"]], "(g) NB-log: Z-AOV-X1")
plot_hist_pvalues(post_aov_x1_pvals[["NB-linear"]], post_aov_x1_ub[["NB-linear"]], "(h) NB-linear: Z-AOV-X1")
Code
par(op)

15 Diagnostic P-value Summary

The table reports the same one-dataset diagnostic workflow for all four models. For posterior and ISCV Z-residual tests, the entries are upper-bound p-values summarizing 500 replicated RSP Z-residual p-values. PPC and HPC entries are the corresponding predictive-check p-values. The most important targeted diagnostic here is Z-AOV-X1, because the deliberate functional-form error is tied to the effect of x1.

16 Interpretation

The HNB-log model is the reference case because it uses both the data-generating response family and the data-generating logarithmic effect of x1. Its residual plots should look comparatively structureless, and the targeted Z-AOV-X1 p-values should not show systematic evidence of a residual mean shift across x1 groups.

The HNB-linear model isolates a functional-form error. A small Z-AOV-X1 p-value for this model indicates that replacing the logarithmic effect with a linear effect leaves a systematic residual pattern against x1. This is the main advantage of covariate-specific Z-residual diagnostics: they can identify where the model is wrong, rather than only saying that the overall fit is inadequate.

The NB-log model does not isolate only a response-family error. Because the HNB data-generating process has a covariate-dependent zero/count mechanism, fitting an ordinary NB model can project this omitted hurdle structure into the NB mean function. Consequently, a Z-AOV-X1 rejection for the NB-log model is meaningful: it reflects the effective functional-form distortion induced by the wrong response family, not an inconsistency in the diagnostic. The zero-count indicators in the NB residual plots are useful even though the NB models do not explicitly contain a hurdle component: isolation or over-abundance of small residuals among zeros can reveal errors in modelling the distribution of zero counts. The NB-linear model combines the response-family misspecification with an explicitly wrong linear functional form and can therefore be flagged by both overall and covariate-specific diagnostics.

Taken together, the demo illustrates a practical residual workflow for Bayesian discrete regression: use Z-residual plots to see the structure of the misfit, use replicated Z-residual p-values and upper-bound summaries for discrete responses, and compare the conclusions with PPC and HPC checks. These results also suggest that different residual diagnostics may respond to different sources of model misspecification. Developing diagnostic procedures that can systematically distinguish among misspecified mean structure, zero-generating mechanism, and count distributional form is an interesting direction for future work and would require dedicated simulation studies.
